summary: Specifies algorithm identifiers and ASN.1 encodings for digital signatures and subject public keys used in the Internet X.509 PKI. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Certificates must say which math method they use. This gives the official names and formats for those methods.

questions: what oid does rsa use in a certificate
how are ecdsa public keys encoded in certificates
subtitle: The names and byte layouts certificates use to say which hash, signature and public key algorithms they rely on.

tldr.problem: An X.509 certificate or revocation list has to say exactly which algorithm signed it and which kind of public key it carries, and every implementation must write and read those declarations the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns an object identifier (OID) to each hash, signature and key algorithm and defines the ASN.1 structures and parameter rules for RSA, DSA, Diffie-Hellman, KEA and elliptic curve keys and signatures.
tldr.outcome: It supplements RFC 3280 and is a Proposed Standard that later documents have updated, so it is a base reference for algorithm identifiers rather than the last word.

today: RFC 3279 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 4055, RFC 4491, RFC 5480, RFC 5758 and RFC 8692, which are the places to look for later algorithm identifiers. It is not marked obsoleted in the metadata for this page.

sections.title: What the Profile Adds
sections.content:
RFC 3279 supplements RFC 3280, the Internet X.509 certificate and CRL profile, and implementations of it MUST also conform to RFC 3280. It defines the contents of four fields in certificates and CRLs: signatureAlgorithm, signatureValue, signature and subjectPublicKeyInfo.

Two jobs are covered. First, it names the one-way hash functions and signature algorithms that sign certificates and CRLs: RSA, DSA and ECDSA. Second, it gives the encoding for the public key in a certificate for RSA, DSA, Diffie-Hellman, KEA, ECDSA and ECDH.

Conforming CAs and applications MUST, at a minimum, support digital signatures and public keys for one of the specified algorithms. Whenever they use one of these algorithms, they MUST support it as described.
sections.eli5: RFC 3280 says what goes on a certificate. This document says how to write down the secret-code methods on it, so everyone reads them the same way.

sections.title: One-Way Hash Functions
sections.content:
A signature is computed over a short fingerprint of the data, made by a one-way hash function, also called a message digest algorithm. The profile includes three: MD2, MD5 and SHA-1. SHA-1 is the preferred one. It produces a 160-bit hash.

MD2 and MD5 each produce a 128-bit hash. They are included because PEM uses MD2 for certificates and MD5 appears in other legacy applications. The RFC says the use of both for new applications is discouraged, though it is still reasonable to use them to verify existing signatures.

For MD2 the RFC cites an attack presented at the Selected Areas in Cryptography '95 conference that can nearly find collisions. For MD5 it mentions pseudo-collisions and no other known cryptanalytic results.
sections.eli5: A hash is a fingerprint of a message. SHA-1 is the favorite fingerprint maker here, and the older MD2 and MD5 are only kept so old stamps can still be checked.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms and Their Identifiers
sections.content:
A certificate or CRL names its signature algorithm in the signatureAlgorithm field, as an OID with optional parameters. Signature algorithms are always used with a one-way hash function. The signature value is ASN.1 encoded as a BIT STRING.

RSA comes in three flavours: md2WithRSAEncryption, md5WithRSAEncryption and sha-1WithRSAEncryption, using the padding and encoding conventions of PKCS #1 (RFC 2313). When any of these OIDs appears in an AlgorithmIdentifier, the parameters field SHALL be the ASN.1 type NULL.

DSA is used with SHA-1 and has the OID id-dsa-with-sha1. ECDSA is used with SHA-1 as ecdsa-with-SHA1. For both, the encoding omits the parameters field, so the identifier is a SEQUENCE of one component. The issuer's key parameters in subjectPublicKeyInfo apply to verifying the signature.

DSA and ECDSA each produce two values, called r and s. They are carried together as a SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs, Dss-Sig-Value for DSA and Ecdsa-Sig-Value for ECDSA.
sections.eli5: Each signing method gets its own name tag. RSA tags carry an empty note, while DSA and ECDSA tags carry no note at all, and the two numbers that make up a DSA or ECDSA signature are packed together in one box.

sections.title: Subject Public Key Algorithms
sections.content:
A certificate also carries the subject's public key, and the key's algorithm is named by an OID in subjectPublicKeyInfo. Conforming CAs MUST use the OIDs given here when issuing certificates with these key types, and applications that support an algorithm MUST at least recognize its OID.

  • RSA: OID rsaEncryption, parameters NULL, key encoded as RSAPublicKey (modulus and public exponent). One key used for both signing and encryption is not recommended, but is not forbidden.
  • DSA: OID id-dsa, with optional domain parameters p, q and g (Dss-Parms). If they are omitted, they come from the issuer if the CA signed with DSA, or by other means otherwise. If they are unavailable, clients MUST reject the certificate. The key is a DER encoded INTEGER.
  • Diffie-Hellman: OID dhpublicnumber, with DomainParameters (p, g, q and optional j and validation parameters). The key is an INTEGER.
  • KEA: OID id-keyExchangeAlgorithm. The parameters field holds an 80-bit domain identifier, made by DER encoding the domain parameters, taking a 160-bit SHA-1 hash, and XORing its high 80 bits with its low 80 bits.
  • ECDSA and ECDH: OID id-ecPublicKey, with parameters chosen from ecParameters (spelled out in full), namedCurve (an OID) or implicitlyCA (NULL, meaning inherited from the issuer). Implementations MUST support the uncompressed point form and MAY support the compressed form.

The keyUsage extension, when present, is limited to values that suit the key type. For DH, KEA and elliptic curve keys it must assert keyAgreement and must not assert both encipherOnly and decipherOnly.
sections.eli5: The certificate also holds the owner's public key, and each kind of key has its own name tag and its own way of being written. Some keys come with a settings sheet, and some borrow the settings of whoever issued the certificate.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
Section 3 collects every definition in one ASN.1 module named PKIX1Algorithms88, written with EXPLICIT TAGS. It repeats the OIDs and structures above in machine-readable form: hash OIDs, DSA, RSA, Diffie-Hellman, KEA and the elliptic curve types, including the finite field types (prime fields and characteristic-two fields with their basis types).

It also lists the named curves from ANSI X9.62 as OIDs: 20 characteristic-two curves such as c2pnb163v1 and seven prime curves from prime192v1 to prime256v1.
sections.eli5: The last big part is a master list that writes every name and layout in a strict computer-readable form, so programs can be built straight from it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not limit the size of public keys or their parameters, but the key size chosen affects the strength achieved, and picking an appropriate size is critical. It also does not name particular elliptic curves, and some curves are cryptographically stronger than others.

It suggests that using well-known curves, such as the named curves from ANSI X9.62, is a sound strategy. The security considerations of RFC 3280 apply here as well.
sections.eli5: The rules do not say how big a secret key must be, but a small key is easier to break, so choose carefully and prefer the well-known recipes.
